rules.why: projects.merge ships, has no phase-1 caller and is exercised by tests only: criterion 3 drives it directly against the command surface. Its inverse, the split, is deferred to phase 4, so a control wired to it is an irreversible join with no undo — the §17 breach §11.1 forbids by name. §22.4's hydration was considered and excluded: it is a third thing, not a merge — one project row existed for the repository throughout, so nothing is absorbed and nothing is tombstoned, and a build in which it called merge_projects would tombstone a row that never existed and let the earliest created_at win, so a blueprint synced on Monday would absorb a local project cloned on Tuesday.
rules.allowWhy: The implementation and its dispatch arm are where the command has to be named. The shell's two entries are tables — the command allowlist the transport enforces and the write/read effect table — and a table is not a caller; the control this rule exists to catch would live in the renderer, which is scanned whole.

rules.why: project.slow_repo is an operator opt-out distinct from deferred_slow, and no phase-1 surface writes it. v2.2 asked for a command to set it and drew no control to call one; the column stands and a later reader must not wire one on the strength of that paragraph.
TRY AGAIN on one tile means one repository. scan.start re-queues the library, and stretching it over the per-project control would rescan everything from a button that promises not to.

Trust is stored in Codotheca's own database and passed per invocation as -c safe.directory=<exact-path>. Writing the user's git config is a write, and §17 permits none; this is the static complement to the byte-identical-config assertion. It reaches argv built outside core/src/git, which the read-only argv audit cannot see because it reads one directory and one literal form.
rules.allowWhy: The corpus generator and the seam fakes build fixture repositories and are gated behind the testkit feature; constructing a repository is their whole job and is not a product git invocation.

rules.why: This rule pins SPAWN SITES rather than subcommand vocabulary: no file outside the three named here constructs a process whose program is git. Auditing the seam instead of the words is what makes it survive phases 3 and 4 unchanged, and it is the complement of no-destructive-git, which matches quoted subcommand literals and therefore cannot see a program name held in a variable. The pattern is a substring, so it catches the fully-qualified std::process::Command::new spelling as well as the bare one — half the real sites in this core use the qualified form, and a matcher that saw only one spelling would let four spawns past while reporting green.
rules.allowWhy: The three allowed files are the git spawn sites: the read seam, the write seam, and the corpus generator behind the testkit feature. The three allowLines are the non-git spawns and are justified per line rather than per file, because allowing their files would make this rule read nothing in them at all — an editor chosen by the user, a launch probe, and wsl.exe. Two further occurrences sit inside #[cfg(test)] mod tests and are removed by stripRustTestModules before this rule sees them.

rules.why: Every git invocation in phase 1 is read-only and argv-only. These subcommands as quoted argv literals are the whole destructive surface, fetch included: a directional claim needs a merge-base across two object stores, which needs a fetch, which §17 forbids. Quoted rather than bare words on purpose — fetch_head_at and reset_at are legitimate column names and a bare-word pattern would fail every correct build.
rules.allowWhy: core/src/git is excluded because core/tests/git_readonly.rs already audits it properly — an allow list plus a deny list over its argv literals, with its own scanned-nothing guard — and a second, weaker grep over the same directory would be the copy that drifts. core/src/gitw is excluded for the same reason and not a weaker one: core/tests/git_write_audit.rs audits it by ENUMERATING Intent::ALL and rendering every variant, which is strictly stronger than this grep — it also asserts the eight-entry flag denylist that no text search over quoted literals can express, because this rule matches subcommand vocabulary and the difference between an additive fetch and a destructive one is a flag. This rule covers what neither audit reaches: argv assembled elsewhere in the core. The corpus generator and the seam fakes build fixture repositories behind the testkit feature.

rules.why: A BASELINE LOCK over every filesystem removal in the core. The single warranted primitive lives in core/src/removal/; every other removal that exists today removes app-owned bytes and is pinned per line, never by a directory wildcard. allow: ["core/src/art/"] would admit an eighteenth call site in an already-listed file silently, which is the whole failure this rule exists to prevent. Its complement is core/tests/removal_audit.rs, which pins the same sites by file AND line number and asserts the total, so even a new call whose text matches an existing allowLine is caught there.
rules.allowWhy: 17 regexes covering the 21 phase-1 and Task-4 sites measured on this tree (four pairs share their text). Every one removes APP-OWNED bytes: a single-instance lock file, a crashed run's own state directory, a temporary or superseded raster, the raster cache, the testkit fixture corpus and its lock, a database backup and its WAL sibling, the credential helper's one-shot socket, nonce and private directory, and the startup-failure breadcrumb. None can reach a user's working copy. BOTH p2-24 Task 11 and p2-24b Task 1 state this baseline as 17: they were written before p2-24's own Task 4 landed the credential helper, whose teardown is the other four. p2-24b must assert 21, not 17.

rules.why: THE STRONG FORM, WHERE IT BITES. remove_dir_all is the only shape that can take a working copy, so it is allowed in four files and no others — the warranted primitive plus the three that recursively remove app-owned trees today. Unlike the baseline lock above this rule has NO allowLines: a new recursive removal outside these four files has no entry available to it and must be routed through remove_warranted.
rules.allowWhy: core/src/removal/ is the single warranted primitive. lifecycle.rs removes a crashed run's own state directory, art/job.rs clears the derived raster cache, and corpus/mod.rs builds and rebuilds the testkit fixture corpus under a temporary root. Six sites across the three.
